Chapter 4.7 (textbook; slides being updated)

Basics of filtering in the frequency domain

TB 4.7kernel → H(u,v)Oct 2024 Q2(ii) = TB 4.47

Your prof’s email puts the syllabus “up to Sec. 4.7”, and the slides for it are not out yet: this section follows the textbook. The exam-style skill: turn a small spatial kernel into H(u,v) and say whether it is lowpass or highpass.

Filtering = multiplication
\[g(x,y)=\mathcal F^{-1}\{H(u,v)F(u,v)\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g=h\circledast f\]
Idea
H scales each frequency. Lowpass H (≈1 near the centre, small far away) blurs; highpass H (small at the centre) sharpens and kills the average (H(0,0) = 0 ⇒ the output has zero mean). The kernel’s DC gain is H(0,0) = sum of the kernel entries.
Watch out
Zero-phase-shift filters: H real and symmetric ⇒ it multiplies the real and imaginary parts of F by the same number ⇒ no phase change ⇒ no geometric distortion.
Remember
Kernel sum = H(0,0) = DC gain.
Steps (textbook 4.7.3)
Idea
  1. Pad the M×N image to P×Q, P ≥ 2M − 1, Q ≥ 2N − 1 (usually P = 2M, Q = 2N) — to avoid wraparound error of circular convolution.
  2. Multiply by \((-1)^{x+y}\) to centre the transform.
  3. DFT → F(u,v).
  4. Multiply by a real, symmetric filter H(u,v) centred at (P/2, Q/2).
  5. Inverse DFT, take the real part (removes round-off imaginary residue).
  6. Multiply by \((-1)^{x+y}\) again.
  7. Crop the top-left M×N region.
Remember
Pad, centre, DFT, multiply, IDFT, real, un-centre, crop.
From a spatial kernel to H(u,v) — the exam skill
\[h=\sum_{(s,t)}w(s,t)\,\delta(x-s,y-t)\ \Rightarrow\ H(u,v)=\sum_{(s,t)}w(s,t)\,e^{-j2\pi(us/M+vt/N)}\]
Idea
Place the kernel centre at the origin. Each tap at (s, t) becomes \(e^{-j2\pi(us/M+vt/N)}\). Symmetric pairs combine into cosines: \(e^{-j\theta}+e^{j\theta}=2\cos\theta\); antisymmetric pairs into sines: \(e^{j\theta}-e^{-j\theta}=2j\sin\theta\).
Watch out
Results to remember (θ = 2πu/M, ψ = 2πv/N): average of the 4 neighbours: \(\tfrac12(\cos\theta+\cos\psi)\); 4-neighbour Laplacian: \(2\cos\theta+2\cos\psi-4\) (≤ 0, zero only at DC); [1 2 1]: \(2(1+\cos\psi)\); [−1 0 1] as correlation (f(x+1) − f(x−1)): \(2j\sin\theta\); first difference f(x+1) − f(x): \(e^{j\theta}-1\).
Remember
Symmetric taps → cosines (real H). Antisymmetric → j·sines.
Gaussian pair
\[H(\mu)=A\,e^{-\mu^2/2\sigma^2}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ h(t)=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma A\,e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2t^2}\]
Idea
Both are Gaussians, with reciprocal widths: a narrow lowpass H (strong blur) means a wide spatial kernel. A highpass can be built as a difference of two Gaussians (DoG).
Remember
Gaussian ↔ Gaussian, widths reciprocal.

Questions on frequency-domain filters

Mid-sem Oct 2024 Q2(ii) = Textbook 4.47

H(u,v) of “average of the N₄ neighbours, excluding the pixel”

Exactly as printed in your paper
Same question, typed out
Find a simplified H(u,v) for the filter that averages the 4-neighbours of a pixel and excludes the pixel itself. What type of filter is it?
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here

Check the type numerically (Degree mode).

  1. H(0,0) = ½(cos 0 + cos 0) = 1; H at u = M/4, v = 0: ½(cos 90 + cos 0) = 0.5; at u = M/2, v = 0: ½(cos 180 + 1) = 0 → falls with frequency: lowpass.
Final answer
\(H(u,v)=\tfrac12\left[\cos\dfrac{2\pi u}{M}+\cos\dfrac{2\pi v}{N}\right]\). Lowpass (smoothing): H(0,0) = 1 (keeps the average) and |H| falls as u, v move away from the origin towards the middle of the band. (At the very corner u = M/2, v = N/2 it reaches −1: the checkerboard pattern is passed with inverted sign — still an averaging filter.)
Full solution
Concept
Kernel = ¼(δ(x+1,y) + δ(x−1,y) + δ(x,y+1) + δ(x,y−1)); transform tap by tap.
  1. \(g(x,y)=\tfrac14[f(x+1,y)+f(x-1,y)+f(x,y+1)+f(x,y-1)]\).
  2. Shift property: \(f(x\pm1,y)\leftrightarrow e^{\pm j2\pi u/M}F\), \(f(x,y\pm1)\leftrightarrow e^{\pm j2\pi v/N}F\).
  3. \(H=\tfrac14[2\cos(2\pi u/M)+2\cos(2\pi v/N)]\).
  4. H(0,0) = 1; H decreases towards u = M/4 (value ½·cos ψ) and beyond: low frequencies pass, high ones are attenuated → lowpass.
Answer
\(H(u,v)=\tfrac12\left[\cos\dfrac{2\pi u}{M}+\cos\dfrac{2\pi v}{N}\right]\). Lowpass (smoothing): H(0,0) = 1 (keeps the average) and |H| falls as u, v move away from the origin towards the middle of the band. (At the very corner u = M/2, v = N/2 it reaches −1: the checkerboard pattern is passed with inverted sign — still an averaging filter.)
Check your own working in the lab
Compre Dec 2025 Q2(a)

From H(u,v) back to the 3×3 kernel; output mean

Exactly as printed in your paper
Same question, typed out
\(H(u,v)=8-2\cos(\tfrac{2\pi}3(u-\tfrac32))-2\cos(\tfrac{2\pi}3(v-\tfrac32))-2\cos(\tfrac{2\pi}3(u+v-3))-2\cos(\tfrac{2\pi}3(u-v))\). Find h (3×3). If f ∈ [0, 255] is filtered by h, what is the mean of the output?
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here

Check H(0,0) (Degree mode, centred variables u = v = 3/2):

  1. 8−2cos(0)−2cos(0)−2cos(0)−2cos(0)EXE → 0 ⇒ DC removed ⇒ output mean 0.
Final answer
\(h=\begin{bmatrix}-1&-1&-1\\-1&8&-1\\-1&-1&-1\end{bmatrix}\) (8-neighbour Laplacian, negated). Output mean = 0 (H at DC = 0).
Full solution
Concept
The printed H is written in centred frequency coordinates (u − M/2, v − N/2 with M = N = 3): replace u − 3/2 → u and v − 3/2 → v (note u + v − 3 = (u − 3/2) + (v − 3/2)). Then read the taps off: each \(-2\cos\) term is a symmetric pair of −1 taps.
  1. Uncentred: \(H=8-2\cos\tfrac{2\pi u}3-2\cos\tfrac{2\pi v}3-2\cos\tfrac{2\pi(u+v)}3-2\cos\tfrac{2\pi(u-v)}3\).
  2. 8 = centre tap. \(-2\cos(2\pi u/3)\) = taps −1 at (±1, 0); \(-2\cos(2\pi v/3)\) = taps −1 at (0, ±1); \(-2\cos(2\pi(u+v)/3)\) = −1 at (1,1), (−1,−1); \(-2\cos(2\pi(u-v)/3)\) = −1 at (1,−1), (−1,1).
  3. The mean of the output is H(0,0) × the mean of the input (the DC term is just scaled by H(0,0)). H(0,0) = 8 − 8 = 0 (the kernel sums to 0) ⇒ output mean 0.
Answer
\(h=\begin{bmatrix}-1&-1&-1\\-1&8&-1\\-1&-1&-1\end{bmatrix}\) (8-neighbour Laplacian, negated). Output mean = 0 (H at DC = 0).
Common mistakes
  • Reading the shifted cosines literally (that gives +1 at the N₄ taps and a kernel summing to 8). Recognise the centred variables first.
Compre 2023-24 Q1

Sobel as two 1-D masks, their spatial expressions and H(u,v)

Exactly as printed in your paper
Same question, typed out
Sobel \(g_x=[-1\,-2\,-1;0\,0\,0;1\,2\,1]\), \(g_y=[-1\,0\,1;-2\,0\,2;-1\,0\,1]\) (x down, y right). Write \(g_x=g_{x1}\star g_{x2}\), \(g_y=g_{y1}\star g_{y2}\): (a) the 1-D masks, (b) the spatial expressions, (c) the frequency responses (DFT \(\sum f e^{-j2\pi(ux/M+vy/N)}\)).
fx-991CW makes this much faster — how to use it here

Symbolic — no calculator.

  1. Multiply the two 1-D responses: 2j sin(2πu/M) × 2(1 + cos(2πv/N)).
Final answer
(a) \(g_{x1}=[1\ 2\ 1]\) (row), \(g_{x2}=[-1\ 0\ 1]^T\) (column); \(g_{y1}=[-1\ 0\ 1]\) (row), \(g_{y2}=[1\ 2\ 1]^T\) (column). (b) \(g_{x1}(x,y)=f(x,y-1)+2f(x,y)+f(x,y+1)\), \(g_{x2}=f(x+1,y)-f(x-1,y)\); \(g_{y1}=f(x,y+1)-f(x,y-1)\), \(g_{y2}=f(x-1,y)+2f(x,y)+f(x+1,y)\). (c) \(H_{x1}=2(1+\cos\frac{2\pi v}N)\), \(H_{x2}=2j\sin\frac{2\pi u}M\), \(H_x=4j\sin\frac{2\pi u}M\big(1+\cos\frac{2\pi v}N\big)\); \(H_{y1}=2j\sin\frac{2\pi v}N\), \(H_{y2}=2(1+\cos\frac{2\pi u}M)\), \(H_y=4j\sin\frac{2\pi v}N\big(1+\cos\frac{2\pi u}M\big)\).
Full solution
Concept
Sobel is separable (rank 1): derivative ⊗ smoothing. Product of the 1-D responses = 2-D response.
  1. Rows of \(g_x\) are −1, 0, +1 times (1 2 1): column [−1 0 1]ᵀ times row [1 2 1].
  2. Spatial expressions as the key writes them (applying the masks as correlations, f(x+1) − f(x−1)).
  3. Each tap pair → cos or j·sin; multiply. The key’s expanded form \(2j\sin2\pi(\frac uM+\frac vN)+4j\sin\frac{2\pi u}M+2j\sin2\pi(\frac uM-\frac vN)\) equals the product above (sum-to-product).
The question calls ⋆ “convolution” but its key applies the masks as correlations. With true convolution every derivative mask flips sign (H gets a factor −1). Magnitudes and the filter type (highpass along one axis, lowpass along the other) are the same.
Answer
(a) \(g_{x1}=[1\ 2\ 1]\) (row), \(g_{x2}=[-1\ 0\ 1]^T\) (column); \(g_{y1}=[-1\ 0\ 1]\) (row), \(g_{y2}=[1\ 2\ 1]^T\) (column). (b) \(g_{x1}(x,y)=f(x,y-1)+2f(x,y)+f(x,y+1)\), \(g_{x2}=f(x+1,y)-f(x-1,y)\); \(g_{y1}=f(x,y+1)-f(x,y-1)\), \(g_{y2}=f(x-1,y)+2f(x,y)+f(x+1,y)\). (c) \(H_{x1}=2(1+\cos\frac{2\pi v}N)\), \(H_{x2}=2j\sin\frac{2\pi u}M\), \(H_x=4j\sin\frac{2\pi u}M\big(1+\cos\frac{2\pi v}N\big)\); \(H_{y1}=2j\sin\frac{2\pi v}N\), \(H_{y2}=2(1+\cos\frac{2\pi u}M)\), \(H_y=4j\sin\frac{2\pi v}N\big(1+\cos\frac{2\pi u}M\big)\).
Calculator · allowed in the mid-sem (scientific, non-programmable)

Your fx-991CW for DIP

every recipe worked on a real questionnumbers computed independently

Each recipe below: what it computes, why the matrices you type are the right ones, a step-by-step run on an actual question from your papers (what you press → what you enter → what the screen shows), and the rule to build the same thing for any other matrix in the exam.

Set up once

  • Angle unit Degree: SETTINGS→Calc Settings→Angle Unit→Degree (cos(120) etc. and 1∠θ).
  • Store intermediate values with STOA …; a matrix cell can hold the letter A.
  • Round only the final answer (your instructor reports 4 decimals).

Matrix app — the only five moves you need

  • Open: HOME→Matrix→OK. Variables MatA, MatB, MatC, MatD, each up to 4×4, real numbers only.
  • Define: TOOLS→MatA→OK→Define New → choose rows, columns → type each cell + EXE (expressions like √3÷2, cos(120), π are fine).
  • Use in a calculation: CATALOG→Matrix→MatB (or the on-screen variable list).
  • Transpose / inverse / determinant: CATALOG→Matrix→Matrix Calc → Transposition (Trn) / x⁻¹ / Determinant.
  • Save a result for reuse: TOOLS→Store→MatD (the last result is also in MatAns).
Quick map: histogram numbers → A, B · filtering → C (whole image) or C′ (one pixel) · DFT → D (matrix) or E (complex) · geometry & interpolation → F · bits → G · Gaussian values → H.

A · Mean and standard deviation from a histogram — Statistics app

What it does. gives the image mean m and σ straight from the counts.
Why it works. the normalised histogram is a probability distribution of grey levels; the Statistics app with a frequency column computes exactly \(m=\sum r\,p(r)\) and \(\sigma=\sqrt{\sum (r-m)^2p(r)}\) (σx divides by the total count, which is what an image σ means).

Why it works. \(s_k=(L-1)\sum_{j\le k}n_j/MN\). Column B accumulates the counts with one copied formula; column C scales them. Using counts (not rounded probabilities) avoids rounding drift.

C · A whole filtered image in one line — band matrices

What it does. filters an image of up to 4×4 with a separable kernel (box, weighted mean, Gaussian, Sobel) or a Laplacian, all output pixels at once.
Why it works. A separable kernel is a column u times a row v: \(w = u\,v^T\). Multiplying \(T\,f\) with the band matrix \(T\) (row i: u₋₁ in column i−1, u₀ on the diagonal, u₁ in column i+1) makes row i of the result \(u_{-1}f_{i-1}+u_0f_i+u_1f_{i+1}\) — the 1-D filter run down every column. Multiplying by \(T^T\) on the right runs it along every row. Both together = the 2-D filter. Padding only decides what happens to the term that falls outside: zero padding drops it; replicate padding adds its weight to the edge pixel, i.e. to the corner entry of T.

Do it on any question
  • Build T for any 3-tap kernel (u₋₁, u₀, u₁) and size n ≤ 4: row i has u₋₁ at column i−1, u₀ at i, u₁ at i+1 (drop what falls outside).
  • Padding → corners: zero: nothing. Replicate (= symmetric for 3×3): T(0,0) += u₋₁ and T(n−1,n−1) += u₁. Mirror (reflect): T(0,1) += u₋₁ and T(n−1,n−2) += u₁.
  • Correlation uses u as printed; convolution: reverse u (and v). For symmetric u (1 2 1 / 1 1 1 / Gaussian) both are the same.
  • Which u, v? weighted mean: ¼(1,2,1) both · box: ⅓(1,1,1) both · Gaussian: (a,1,a)/(1+2a) both · Sobel gₓ (rows differ): u = (−1,0,1), v = (1,2,1) · Sobel g_y: u = (1,2,1), v = (−1,0,1).
  • Non-square m×n (e.g. 3×4): Tu is m×m, Tv is n×n: MatB×MatA×Trn(MatC). Quiz-1 Q1’s whole 3×4 Gaussian output is one product (see its card).
  • Laplacians: 4-neighbour = D f + f D (replicate: D’s corner −2 → −1). 8-neighbour = T₁ f T₁ − 9f with T₁ from (1,1,1). Sharpened g = f − ∇²f: one more subtraction.
  • Image bigger than 4×4 (e.g. 5×5): use C′ below pixel by pixel.

C′ · One output pixel — separable trick or trace trick

What it does. one filtered pixel g(x,y) with any 3×3 kernel, from its 3×3 window.
Why it works. Separable \(w = u\,v^T\): \(\sum_{s,t}w(s,t)W(s,t)=u^T W v\) — a row times the window times a column. Any kernel K: the sum of the Hadamard product equals \(\mathrm{trace}(W^TK)\) — the diagonal of \(W^T K\) holds exactly the column-by-column dot products.

D · DFT coefficients with real matrices

What it does. F(u,v) (real part, imaginary part, magnitude) of an image up to 4×4 — or of the non-zero 3×3 block of a bigger image.
Why it works. \(F(u,v)=\sum_x\sum_y f(x,y)\,W_m^{ux}W_n^{vy}\) with \(W^k=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta\). Write \(c_u(x)=\cos(360°\,ux/m)\), \(s_u(x)=\sin(360°\,ux/m)\) (and the same in y). Then \(F=(c_u-is_u)^Tf\,(c_v-is_v)=c_u^Tfc_v-s_u^Tfs_v-i\,(c_u^Tfs_v+s_u^Tfc_v)\). Stacking \([c_u;s_u]\) as a 2-row matrix and \([c_v\ s_v]\) as a 2-column matrix, one product gives all four pieces: P = [[c f c, c f s],[s f c, s f s]].

Do it on any question
  • Affine: any 3 non-collinear pairs. Map a new point: A × (x, y, 1)ᵀ. Inverse mapping: A⁻¹ × (x′, y′, 1)ᵀ.
  • Registration (4 tie points): two 4-unknown systems — rows (v, w, vw, 1 | x) for c₁…c₄ and (v, w, vw, 1 | y) for c₅…c₈.
  • Circular convolution of length n ≤ 4; for n > 4 use the linear-then-wrap method by hand.

G · Bit planes and Gray code — Base-N app

What it does. the binary (or Gray) digits of a pixel value.
Why it works. Bit plane k = bit k of the binary representation; Gray code g = b XOR (b shifted right by 1).
Worked on Quiz-1 Q2 (top 3 planes) and Oct 2024 Q3(i) (Gray)

Do it on any question
  • Top t planes of a k-bit value r: 2^(k−t) × (r ÷ 2^(k−t) with decimals dropped).
  • Gray MSB = binary MSB; build the 0–7 Gray table once and read every pixel from it.

H · Gaussian kernel values — Table app

What it does. the edge and corner weights of a Gaussian for any σ.
Why it works. G(s,t) = e^{−(s²+t²)/2σ²}: edge (distance 1) = a, corner (distance √2) = a², next ring = a⁴…
Worked on Quiz-1 Q1, σ = 0.7

Do it on any question
  • 3×3: centre 1, edges f(1), corners f(1)²; sum (1 + 2f(1))².
  • 5×5: also f(2) and the mixed products f(1)f(2), f(2)².

Your two-sided A4 cheat sheet

copy by hand, very smallcovers every question type

Copy this onto the two sides of your A4 sheet. Side 1 = chapters 1–3, side 2 = chapter 4, the calculator recipes and a traps checklist. It is built so that any question in this guide can be solved from the sheet alone: procedures, the tables you would otherwise derive (Gaussian values, cos/sin of DFT angles, D₃/D₄, Gray codes) and the conventions that cost marks.

Traps checklist☐ which index base? ☐ corr or conv? ☐ which padding? ☐ normalise kernel (÷ sum) ☐ σ² in Gaussian ☐ DFT with or without 1/mn (printed formula wins) ☐ W has minus sign ☐ histogram: Σn = MN check ☐ matching tie → smallest z ☐ round only at the end ☐ clip to 0…L−1 if output must be k-bit ☐ odd-size centring ≠ (−1)^{x+y} ☐ σx not sx
Tips: write with a 0.3–0.5 mm pen; use abbreviations from the sheet; draw the D₄ matrix and the Gray table exactly as shown. Re-solve two cards (e.g. Quiz-1 Q1, Oct 2023 Q1) using only your sheet to test that nothing is missing.
